Takes the music off the line between your ears.

Headphones put the music inside your head. This puts it in front of you instead.\n\nHeadphones does it in the app, so it works on any phone. Surround upmix asks your phone to do it, which only helps if your phone supports it.
How far apart the two virtual speakers are. 30 degrees is what stereo is mixed for.\n\nWider separates the instruments more. Too wide leaves a gap in the middle.

The music stays where it is when you turn your head.\n\nNeeds headphones that report which way they are facing, and a phone that shares it. Most phones do not, so this is hidden unless yours does.
How far ahead of your head the sound aims.

Sound takes time to reach your ears, so the app aims slightly ahead of your head.\n\nQuick and Instant feel immediate but can overshoot when you stop turning. Smooth never overshoots but feels slightly behind.
Treats your phone as where the music is coming from.

Your phone becomes where the music comes from. Walk away and it gets quieter.\n\nIt judges distance from Bluetooth signal strength, which is rough, so it changes slowly and only a little. It never mutes.
Check how well distance can be measured where you are.

A 100 second test to check this works where you are. It reads each step out loud, so you can put the phone down and follow along.\n\nIf turning on the spot moves the signal as much as walking away does, distance cannot be measured here.
Stay where you are and turn slowly on the spot.
Leave the phone and walk as far away as you can.
Finished. You can pick the phone up.
Looking up, down or sideways moves the sound as well.
Looking up and down moves the sound too, not just turning.\n\nUses a bit more battery, and restarts the current song when you switch it on.
Not calibrated. Tap, then look straight ahead and keep still.

resources.string: Correcting %1$.2f degrees per second of drift.
Your headphones slowly lose track of which way is forward, so the music drifts to one side.\n\nSit still and look straight ahead for 30 seconds. It measures your drift and corrects it from then on.
How far ahead the sound aims, in milliseconds. It should match the delay to your ears, which depends on your Bluetooth codec.\n\nPlay something, turn your head, and drag until the sound stays put.
Process volume and effects in 32-bit instead of 16-bit.
Volume normalisation changes every sample, and in 16-bit the result is rounded afterwards. 32-bit avoids that rounding. It costs some battery and the difference is small, so this is a preference.

No Home row shows a song an earlier row already has, and versions of one song (live, remastered, video) count as the same. Nothing fills a gap, so a row can come up short. Off, your exclusions only filter the Best recommendations row.

Puts the Quick picks row in an order that suits you: songs you play often, played lately or liked tend to come first. Nothing is added or removed. It leaves the row alone when Best recommendations or Try both fills it.

The row is twenty cards: songs related to what you play, songs you keep coming back to, more from your artists, old favourites gone quiet, and a few new to you. These settings apply while Quick picks source is Best recommendations or Try both.

Higher gives more of the row to songs new to you: one card of twenty at 0, two at 50, three at 100. The other kinds of card make room. A change shows the next time the row is made, or when you pull down on Home.
Higher gives more of the row to songs you got into in the last two weeks: none at 0, four cards of twenty at 25, up to eleven at 60. The other kinds of card make room.

Where Best recommendations and Discover something new find songs like the ones you play. With Both or Last.fm only, the title and artist of songs you play or have liked go to Last.fm, nothing else and no account. YouTube only sends Last.fm nothing.
Both starts half and half. The source whose songs you play more of gets more of the places, up to four in five, and the other always keeps one in five so it can win them back.

The whole row goes to songs you have not heard past about halfway; one you skipped early still counts as new. Adventurousness and Familiarity stop mattering while it is on. The row can come up short, and Quick picks then shows another source.
Each card says the main reason it is there: a song it goes with, an artist you play, a like, or that it is new to you. A wildcard is a card picked at random to keep the row fresh.

Long-press a card in Quick picks for Not this song, Less of this artist (for a month) or Never this artist. They only filter the recommendation rows, never search, your library or playlists. This page lists what is in force, and Lift removes one.

Skip a song you like or play often before its halfway point, and it stays out of the Best recommendations row for a week. A skip in the first thirty seconds does not count. You can lift a rest early on the Exclusions page.
A rested song is also kept out of the other Home rows, not only Best recommendations. Those rows can come back shorter. It needs Tidy Home rows on.
Learn from listening decides whether it learns at all. Rests and exclusions keep songs out of the row: a rest lasts a week after a skip, an exclusion as long as you chose.
Worked out on this phone from your own listening, and nothing leaves it unless you save a copy under Your data. Give it a few weeks before you read much into the numbers.
What it has learned is kept on this phone. Here you can take back a session or a day, reset or rebuild it, and save or load a copy. Anything that changes it asks first.

Seen means a card was on screen for half a second, or you tapped it. Played means you heard a good part of that song, or liked it. A card you did not tap is judged a day later, so the newest are not counted yet.
Worked out on this phone from your own listening; nothing leaves it unless you save a copy under Your data. Give it a few weeks: a card is judged a day late, and it learns only a little each day.

Each card it showed you is judged against what you did next, and that nudges how it scores cards like it. Off, it stops learning; your plays are still logged, so History and Stats are untouched. It all runs on the phone.
Of the cards each source showed you, how many you went on to play. Every source is counted by the same rules, so the lines can be compared. A card you did not tap waits a day before it counts.

The unseen row is built when Home opens and is never shown. A day later it is checked against what you went on to play; it teaches Best recommendations nothing. Off, the unseen line on this page stops filling in.

A day after a row changes, the app looks at the songs you chose to play in the meantime. A song counts as held when it was already in that row. Expect low numbers: the row had to guess what you would pick on your own.

Every card it shows carries its guess at how likely you are to play it. The first line puts the average guess beside how many were played: the closer the two, the better. The lines under it group the cards by the chance it gave them.

Each line is one weight, with its starting value in brackets. Above its start, that feature pushes a card\'s score up more; below, it pushes it down more. Read each against its own start, not against the others.
It goes back to how it started, as if it had learned nothing. Your listens, exclusions and settings are kept, and Rebuild what it learned brings the learning back. It asks first.

It starts from the beginning and learns again from every card it has shown you, leaving out what you told it to forget. Use it after a Reset, or after loading a copy. It asks first, and a long history takes longer.

Takes back the session of what is playing now, or of your last play: its listens stop teaching, and what it learned is worked out again without them. It asks first, saying how many listens. History, Stats and play counts are untouched.

Every play started since midnight stops teaching, and what it learned is worked out again without them. It asks first, saying how many listens. A song that began before midnight belongs to yesterday and stays.

The engine\'s constants, each with its default: a number overrides one, an empty field restores it. They change the Best recommendations row only, not what it learns. Pull down on Home to see a change.
Saves what it has learned as a file of numbers, where you choose. No song titles, artists, play counts or dates, and nothing about your account or phone. Nothing is uploaded.

Everything below is what it learns from, kept in the app on this phone and never uploaded. A backup includes it. Under Privacy and history, Pause listen history stops it being written and Clear listen history deletes it.

Best recommendations does not go by what counts as a play. It weighs each listen by how much of the song you heard: under thirty seconds counts for nothing unless you liked it. Skips matter to it as much as songs you finished.

A session is a run of listening with no gap longer than thirty minutes. The row starts from the session you are in, and a song counts at most three times per session, so an hour on repeat does not outweigh a week.

How each listen stopped: played to the end, skipped by you, replaced by a new queue, failed, or simply stopped. A song you heard only ever counts in its favour, and a skip counts against it, at most half as much. A play that failed teaches it nothing.

Each place counts the times you started playing from there; the songs that play on after are not counted again. A song you chose yourself teaches it more than one that just played on, and a search counts most. Not recorded means the app did not note where it began.

A card counts as seen when half of it stayed on screen for half a second after you stopped scrolling. Only the cards of Best recommendations and Discover something new teach it anything. A card seen and not played within a day counts a little against that song.
Each is stored with the moment it happened, and never leaves the phone. They are kept, not used: nothing that picks or orders your cards reads them yet. Pause listen history stops all of it.

The last thirty listens it learns from, newest first. Each line says how the play ended, how much of the song you heard and where it was started from. Not learned from means you told it to forget that listen.

The first chip is your usual row. The others lean it for now: Discover toward songs new to you, Favourites toward what you have liked, and Focus, Chill and Party toward what you play while each is on. A chip stays on until you change it.

Where the Quick picks row gets its songs. YouTube Music uses the shelf YouTube makes for your account, and Your library uses songs related to what you play. Only this row changes, nothing else on Home.
